Module 6 Assignment - Linear Regression Methods¶

California Housing Price Prediction Using Linear Regression

Created By - Tushar Ahuja

Introduction¶

The housing market is a critical pillar of any nation’s economy, influencing financial stability, urban development, and individual investment decisions. Understanding and accurately predicting housing prices is essential for various stakeholders, including homebuyers, real estate investors, government agencies, and policymakers.

This assignment aims to leverage machine learning techniques to build a robust predictive model for median housing prices in California. The dataset, published by the US Census Bureau, contains information from 20,640 districts (block groups)—the smallest geographical units used for census data collection. Each district represents a population ranging from 600 to 3,000 people and includes 10 key metrics, such as:

  • Population density
  • Median income
  • Median housing price
  • Proximity to amenities
  • Household characteristics

By analyzing these variables, the model will learn patterns in the data and predict median housing values across districts. This predictive capability will assist various entities in market analysis, urban planning, real estate investment, and financial risk assessment.

Why is Housing Price Prediction Important?

Accurate price forecasting serves multiple purposes:

  • Buyers & Sellers – Helps negotiate fair deals based on market trends
  • Investors – Guides profitable real estate investments and risk mitigation
  • Government Agencies – Supports urban development policies and housing affordability programs
  • Financial Institutions – Aids in loan approvals and mortgage risk assessments

Learning Objectives¶

The goal of this assignment is to develop a Linear Regression Model that predicts median house values in California based on census data provided by the US Census Bureau. The dataset contains 20,640 observations, each representing a block group in California with several attributes such as population, median income, median house age, total rooms, and ocean proximity.

This assignment follows a structured data science approach, which includes:

  • Understanding and Cleaning the Data – Handling missing values and converting categorical data into numerical values.
  • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) – Analyzing patterns, distributions, and correlations between features and housing prices.
  • Building and Evaluating the Model – Implementing Linear Regression, training it on data, and evaluating its performance.
  • Model Diagnostics – Examining residual plots, Q-Q plots, and error distributions to check model validity.

At the end of this project, we will:

  • Gain an in-depth understanding of Linear Regression and its assumptions.
  • Learn how to handle missing values and encode categorical variables.
  • Perform Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) to identify key insights.
  • Train a Linear Regression Model to predict housing prices.
  • Evaluate the model using MSE, RMSE, MAE, and R² score.
  • Interpret residual plots, Q-Q plots, and actual vs. predicted plots for model validation.

Steps Followed in the Project¶

1. Data Preprocessing

  • Load the dataset.
  • Handle missing values by imputing them with the mean.
  • Encode categorical variables into numerical values.
  • Analyse the data further.

2. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

  • Understand the dataset using summary statistics.
  • Visualize the distribution of key variables.
  • Identify correlations between features and the target variable.

3. Building the Linear Regression Model

  • Split the dataset into training and test sets.
  • Train a linear regression model using the training set.
  • Evaluate its performance on the test set.

4. Model Evaluation

  • Calculate Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and R² score.
  • Analyze the significance of these metrics.

5. Model Diagnostics

  • Plot actual vs. predicted values.
  • Generate residual plots to check for homoscedasticity.
  • Create Q-Q plots to assess normality of residuals.
  • Interpret the results to determine if the model requires improvements.

Categorical features represent attributes with discrete values, typically used for classification models after encoding. (Examples Below)

  • ocean_proximity: proximity of the ocean (Near Bay, Island, Inland, Near Ocean).

B. Numerical Features: Numerical data are numbers, not words or descriptions. Can say continuous variables.

numerical_features = df.select_dtypes(include=['int64', 'float64']).columns.tolist()

Numerical Features: ['longitude', 'latitude', 'housing_median_age', 'total_rooms', 'total_bedrooms', 'population', 'households', 'median_income', 'median_house_value']

Explanation¶

Numerical features represent geographical, demographic, and economic attributes that influence housing prices, demand, and affordability.

  • longitude – Continuous variable representing the district's geographical longitude, influencing housing location trends.
  • latitude – Continuous variable representing the district's geographical latitude, affecting spatial analysis of housing prices.
  • housing_median_age – Continuous variable indicating the median age of houses in a district, influencing property valuation.
  • total_rooms – Discrete variable representing the total number of rooms in all district houses, reflecting housing density.
  • total_bedrooms – Discrete variable indicating the total number of bedrooms in a district, impacting housing availability.
  • population – Discrete variable showing the total district population, influencing demand and housing prices.
  • households – Discrete variable representing the number of households in a district, linked to residential density.
  • median_income – Continuous variable representing the median income of residents, strongly correlated with housing prices.
  • median_house_value – Continuous target variable indicating the median house price in a district, used for price prediction.

1.11 Identifying Features: Key Attributes and Descriptions¶

A. Features in the California Housing Dataset¶

  • longitude (Numerical - float): Geographic coordinate representing the east-west location of the district.

  • latitude (Numerical - float): Geographic coordinate representing the north-south location of the district.

  • housing_median_age (Numerical - int): The median age of houses in the district.

  • total_rooms (Numerical - int): The total number of rooms in the district.

  • total_bedrooms (Numerical - int): The total number of bedrooms in the district (contains some missing values).

  • population (Numerical - int): The total number of people residing in the district.

  • households (Numerical - int): The total number of households in the district.

  • median_income (Numerical - float): The median income of households in the district, measured in tens of thousands of dollars ($10,000s).

  • median_house_value (Numerical - int): The target variable – represents the median house price in the district (in USD).

  • ocean_proximity (Categorical - string): Describes the district’s proximity to the ocean, with categories such as:

        - <1H OCEAN → Houses within one hour of the ocean.
    - INLAND → Houses away from coastal areas.
    - NEAR OCEAN → Houses near the ocean but not directly on the coast.
    - NEAR BAY → Houses close to a bay area.
    - ISLAND → Houses located on an island (very rare category).

B. Understanding Feature Importance¶

Each feature contributes differently to the prediction of house prices. Below is a breakdown of why each feature is important:

1. Geographical Features:

  • longitude & latitude → House prices vary by location. Proximity to major cities, beaches, and employment hubs influences pricing significantly.

2. Housing Characteristics:

  • housing_median_age → Newer houses tend to have higher prices than older homes.
  • total_rooms & total_bedrooms → Larger houses with more rooms are generally valued higher, but extreme values may indicate multi-family housing units.

3. Demographic Factors:

  • population & households → High population density areas can increase demand, affecting house prices.

4. Economic Indicators:

  • median_income → Strongest predictor of house prices. Areas with higher median income typically have more expensive houses.

Proximity to the Ocean:

  • ocean_proximity → Coastal properties tend to be more expensive due to demand for scenic views and waterfront access.

C. Key Takeaways¶

  • median_income is the most important factor affecting house prices due to its strong correlation with house values.
  • Location (longitude, latitude) significantly impacts pricing, especially in coastal or high-demand areas.
  • Housing characteristics like age, size, and number of rooms contribute, but their influence is secondary to economic factors.
  • Proximity to the ocean is a key factor, as coastal properties tend to be more expensive.

Explanation:¶

  • The column ocean_proximity is categorical and cannot be directly used in machine learning models.
  • One-Hot Encoding creates new binary columns for each category.

Derived Features (After Encoding)¶

Since machine learning models require numerical inputs, the categorical variable ocean_proximity is converted into binary (0/1) features using One-Hot Encoding. The new features created are:

  • ocean_proximity_<1H OCEAN> (Categorical - 0/1): 1 if the district is within 1 hour of the ocean, else 0.
  • ocean_proximity_INLAND (Categorical - 0/1): 1 if the district is inland, else 0.
  • ocean_proximity_NEAR OCEAN (Categorical - 0/1): 1 if the district is near the ocean, else 0.
  • ocean_proximity_NEAR BAY (Categorical - 0/1): 1 if the district is near a bay, else 0.
  • ocean_proximity_ISLAND (Categorical - 0/1): 1 if the district is on an island, else 0.

Step 4: Model Evaluation¶

Definitions of Model Evaluation Metrics¶

1. Mean Squared Error (MSE)¶

  • Definition:

MSE measures the average squared difference between actual and predicted values. It penalizes larger errors more than smaller ones due to squaring.

  • Interpretation:
  • A lower MSE indicates better model performance.
  • Since it's in squared units, it is not directly interpretable in the same units as the target variable.

2. Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)¶

  • Definition:

RMSE is the square root of MSE, making it more interpretable since it’s in the same unit as the target variable.

  • Interpretation:
  • RMSE provides an estimate of how much, on average, predictions deviate from actual values.
  • A lower RMSE indicates a better fit.

3. Mean Absolute Error (MAE)¶

  • Definition:

MAE measures the average absolute difference between actual and predicted values. Unlike MSE, it doesn’t square the errors, making it less sensitive to large outliers.

  • Interpretation:
  • MAE is easier to interpret since it represents the average prediction error in actual units.
  • Lower MAE means better model performance.

4. R² Score (Coefficient of Determination)¶

  • Definition:

R² measures how well the independent variables explain the variance in the dependent variable. It ranges from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates a perfect fit.

  • Interpretation:
  • R² = 1 → Perfect fit (all variance explained).
  • R² = 0 → Model explains no variance in the target variable.
  • Higher R² means better explanatory power of the model.

Once the model is trained, we evaluate its performance using four key metrics:

Code:

In [207]:
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score
import numpy as np

# Making predictions on the test set
y_pred = model.predict(X_test_scaled)

# Computing model evaluation metrics
mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred)
rmse = np.sqrt(mse)
mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred)
r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)

# Displaying evaluation metrics
print(f"Mean Squared Error (MSE): {mse}")
print(f"Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): {rmse}")
print(f"Mean Absolute Error (MAE): {mae}")
print(f"R² Score: {r2}")

Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE): 79997.06982121796
Mean Absolute Error (MAE): 59802.84232043988
R² Score: 0.5124315712805353

Interpretation of Results¶

  • MSE (6.4 billion) → Measures the average squared error between actual and predicted values.
  • RMSE (approx 80K) → On average, the model’s predictions are off by about 80,000.
  • MAE (approx 60K) → The average absolute error in predictions is around 60,000.
  • R² Score (0.512) → The model explains 51.2% of the variance in house prices.

Conclusion & Next Steps¶

  • The model performs moderately well, with median_income being the strongest predictor.
  • The error is quite high, suggesting additional features could improve the model.
  • Next Steps: We can perform residual analysis and diagnostic checks to verify model assumptions.

Step 5: Model Diagnostics¶

5.1 Model Diagnostics for the Initial Linear Regression Model¶

In [388]:
# Actual vs. Predicted Values Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.scatterplot(x=y_test, y=y_pred, alpha=0.5)
plt.xlabel("Actual Median House Value ($)")
plt.ylabel("Predicted Median House Value ($)")
plt.title("Actual vs. Predicted House Prices (Initial Linear Regression Model)")
plt.show()

# Residual Plot
residuals = y_test - y_pred

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.histplot(residuals, bins=50, kde=True)
plt.axvline(x=0, color='red', linestyle='--')
plt.xlabel("Residuals")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.title("Residual Distribution (Initial Linear Regression Model)")
plt.show()

# Q-Q Plot (Quantile-Quantile Plot)
sm.qqplot(residuals, line='45', fit=True)
plt.title("Q-Q Plot of Residuals (Initial Linear Regression Model)")
plt.show()

Interpretation¶

1. Actual vs. Predicted Values Plot

  • If points deviate significantly from the diagonal, the model is struggling to make accurate predictions.
  • If there is a systematic pattern, it suggests that some important relationships are not captured by the model.

2. Residual Plot

  • If residuals show a clear pattern, it means the model is missing some non-linear trends.
  • If residuals increase or decrease over predictions, it indicates heteroscedasticity (uneven error variance), which means the model does not perform equally well across different price ranges.

3. Q-Q Plot (Quantile-Quantile Plot)

  • If points fall along the diagonal line, residuals are normally distributed, validating model assumptions.
  • If points deviate significantly from the line, it suggests skewness or heavy tails, meaning the model may not be handling extreme values well.

Key Takeaway¶

  • If the diagnostic tools show no major issues, the model is justified.
  • If patterns exist in residuals or the Q-Q plot shows non-normal residuals, the model may need improvements, such as:
    • Adding non-linear features (Polynomial Regression)
    • Including more predictors (Latitude, Longitude, Ocean Proximity)
    • Using regularization (Ridge/Lasso Regression) to handle variance issues.

5.2 Enhancing Linear Regression with Polynomial Features and Ridge Regularization¶

Below code enhances the linear regression model by introducing non-linearity using Polynomial Regression (degree = 2) with Ridge Regularization to prevent overfitting.

In [222]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

# Using a polynomial transformation to introduce non-linearity
degree = 2  # Quadratic features
poly_model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=1.0))

# Train the polynomial regression model
poly_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Make predictions
y_pred_poly = poly_model.predict(X_test)

# Evaluate the polynomial regression model
mse_poly = mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_poly)
rmse_poly = np.sqrt(mse_poly)
mae_poly = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_poly)
r2_poly = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_poly)

# Display improved model evaluation metrics
improved_model_metrics = {
    "Mean Squared Error (MSE)": mse_poly,
    "Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)": rmse_poly,
    "Mean Absolute Error (MAE)": mae_poly,
    "R² Score": r2_poly
}

print(improved_model_metrics)

{'Mean Squared Error (MSE)': 6107052960.263788, 'Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)': 78147.63566649849, 'Mean Absolute Error (MAE)': 58456.37233968441, 'R² Score': 0.5347149451733284}

Explanation¶

1. Feature Transformation:

  • PolynomialFeatures(degree=2): Expands existing features to include quadratic terms for capturing non-linear relationships.

2. Feature Scaling:

  • StandardScaler(): Ensures all features are standardized, improving model efficiency.

3. Model Training:

  • Ridge(alpha=1.0): Applies L2 regularization to reduce overfitting.

4. Predictions & Evaluation:

  • The trained polynomial regression model is used to predict house prices (y_pred_poly).
  • Performance metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE, R²) are computed to compare with the linear model.

Key Takeaways¶

  • Polynomial Regression improves accuracy by capturing non-linear trends.
  • Regularization (Ridge) prevents overfitting.
  • Better R² score shows improved explanatory power of house price variability.

Interpretation¶

1. Actual vs. Predicted Values Plot

*What It Shows:*

  • The scatter plot compares actual house values (y-axis) with predicted values (x-axis).
  • Ideally, the points should align along a 45-degree diagonal line (perfect predictions).

*Observation:*

  • The model underestimates some high-priced houses.
  • The spread of points suggests that predictions deviate significantly from actual values.

2. Residual Plot

*What It Shows:*

  • The residual plot displays errors (differences between actual and predicted values).
  • Ideally, residuals should be randomly distributed around zero.

*Observation:*

  • The residuals are widely spread, indicating that the model does not perfectly capture variance.
  • The presence of a pattern in residuals suggests that some relationships are non-linear, which the linear model does not capture well.

3. Q-Q Plot (Quantile-Quantile Plot)

*What It Shows:*

  • The Q-Q plot checks if residuals follow a normal distribution.
  • If residuals are normally distributed, points should fall along the diagonal line.

*Observation:*

The residuals deviate from the diagonal line, especially in the tails. This suggests that the model does not fully meet the normality assumption, meaning it may struggle with extreme values.

Final Conclusion:¶

The model needs improvement.

  • The Actual vs. Predicted plot shows large deviations.
  • Residuals are not randomly distributed, suggesting missing non-linear relationships.
  • Q-Q plot indicates that residuals are not normally distributed, which affects the validity of statistical inferences.

*Possible Next Steps for Improvement*

  • Add More Features: Include additional predictors like latitude, longitude, and ocean_proximity to improve the model.

  • Use Polynomial or Non-Linear Models: Linear regression assumes a linear relationship, but real-world house prices may have non-linear trends.

  • Apply Regularization (Ridge/Lasso Regression): Helps in reducing overfitting and improving performance.

5.4 Adding more features¶

When we say "Adding More Features," we mean including additional variables (predictors) that might help improve the model’s ability to predict median house prices more accurately.

Why Add More Features?

Currently, our model is based on only three features:

  1. median_income (Strongest predictor)
  2. total_rooms
  3. housing_median_age

However, housing prices are influenced by many other factors, and excluding them may lead to a less accurate model.

In [371]:
# Selecting additional features including geographic information
selected_features = ['median_income', 'total_rooms', 'housing_median_age', 'latitude', 'longitude']  

# Ensuring that one-hot encoded categorical features (ocean proximity) are also included
ocean_proximity_features = [col for col in df.columns if 'ocean_proximity' in col]  # Extract all encoded categories
selected_features.extend(ocean_proximity_features)  # Add them to our feature list

# Defining independent (X) and dependent (y) variables
X = df[selected_features]
y = df['median_house_value']

# Splitting the dataset (70% training, 30% testing)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

# Standardizing the numerical features
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

# Training the new model with additional features
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

# Evaluating the updated model
y_pred_new = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
r2_new = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_new)

# Displaying new R² Score
print(f"New R² Score: {r2_new}")

New R² Score: 0.6097843951741035

Justification for Model Diagnostics and Enhancements¶

Initially, we built a Linear Regression model to predict median house prices in California. However, after performing model diagnostics using Actual vs. Predicted plots, Residual plots, and Q-Q plots, we observed that the model struggled to capture non-linear relationships, and the residuals showed patterns that indicated model inadequacies.

To address these shortcomings, we proactively enhanced the model by introducing Polynomial Features (degree = 2) to capture non-linear relationships and Ridge Regularization to prevent overfitting. This refinement improved the model’s performance by increasing its R² Score and reducing errors like MSE and RMSE.

Following this, we conducted another round of model diagnostics to verify improvements. While the polynomial model performed better, the residual plots and Q-Q plots still suggested room for further refinement. Based on these insights, we added additional features, such as latitude, longitude, and ocean proximity, to incorporate geographical influences on house prices.

This approach reflects an iterative model improvement strategy, where diagnostic tools guide enhancements, leading to a progressively stronger predictive model. While the original request was to perform diagnostics on the natural linear regression model, our proactive approach ensured better accuracy, lower errors, and improved interpretability of California housing prices

Conclusion¶

This assignment successfully built and evaluated a predictive model for California housing prices using Linear Regression and Polynomial Regression with Ridge Regularization. The initial Linear Regression model provided moderate accuracy (R² = 0.512), with median income emerging as the strongest predictor of house prices. However, diagnostic tools such as residual plots and Q-Q plots revealed that the model failed to fully capture the non-linear relationships in the data, necessitating improvements.

To address this, we introduced Polynomial Regression (degree = 2), which enhanced the model’s performance (R² = 0.534), indicating a better fit. While the Polynomial Model reduced errors, the presence of non-normal residuals and high RMSE (~$78K) suggests that further refinements, such as adding more features (e.g., geographical coordinates, categorical encodings) or exploring advanced models like Decision Trees or Neural Networks, could yield even better predictions.

Additionally, we enhanced the model by incorporating more features, including latitude, longitude, and one-hot encoded ocean_proximity categories, to improve the predictive power. These additional features helped capture geographical influences on housing prices, further refining the model.

Overall, this study demonstrates the power of data-driven modeling in real estate forecasting, while also highlighting the importance of feature selection, model diagnostics, and iterative improvements in machine learning models.
